questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with no family history of colorectal cancer had been scheduled for screening colonoscopy every 10 years. At his most recent examination, a 7-mm tubular adenoma with low-grade dysplasia was identified and completely resected. Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his colonoscopy schedule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No change is needed; continue colonoscopy every 10 years

choices.label: B
choices.text: Shorten the interval to surveillance colonoscopy every 1 to 7 years

choices.label: C
choices.text: Discontinue colonoscopy and perform annual guaiac-based fecal occult blood testing instead

explanation.summary: Identifying an adenomatous polyp shortens the colonoscopy screening interval from every 10 years to every 1 to 7 years.
explanation.whyCorrect: Identifying adenomatous polyps matters because it changes the frequency of colonoscopy cancer screening. Instead of every 10 years, the interval becomes every 1 to 7 years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An adenoma is a neoplastic polyp with malignant potential, so the 10-year average-risk interval no longer applies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct: after removal of an adenomatous polyp the surveillance interval shortens to every 1 to 7 years.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Guaiac-based testing has low sensitivity for polyps and would be a downgrade in surveillance for a patient with a known adenoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prophylactic colectomy is considered in familial adenomatous polyposis, not after removal of a single small tubular adenoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stopping screening after finding a precancerous lesion would forgo the very benefit that colonoscopy provides.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is evaluated for intermittent rectal bleeding and diarrhea. His father underwent colectomy at age 30 years, and a paternal aunt died of colon cancer at age 34 years. Colonoscopy shows more than 500 adenomatous polyps carpeting the colon and rectum, and upper endoscopy shows fundic gland polyps and duodenal adenomas. A germline mutation in which of the following genes is most likely present?

explanation.summary: Familial adenomatous polyposis is caused by germline mutation of the APC tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 5q21-22.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hundreds to a thousand colorectal adenomatous polyps in a young adult with an autosomal dominant family history define familial adenomatous polyposis, which results from germline mutations in the APC tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 5q21-22. These patients also have a high rate of upper gastrointestinal polyps, typically fundic gland polyps and duodenal adenomas, as seen here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct: familial adenomatous polyposis results from germline mutation of APC on chromosome 5q21-22.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MSH2 is a mismatch repair gene mutated in Lynch syndrome, which was formerly called hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer and does not produce hundreds of polyps.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MUTYH-associated polyposis is autosomal recessive and typically produces 10 to 100 polyps rather than more than 500 with a dominant family history.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SMAD4 mutations cause juvenile polyposis syndrome, whose polyps are hamartomatous rather than adenomatous.
whyWrongByChoice.E: STK11 mutations cause Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, which features hamartomatous polyps and mucocutaneous pigmentation.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman had a 9-mm tubular adenoma removed at colonoscopy. She is anxious and asks her physician what would have happened to the polyp if it had been left alone. Which of the following statements best describes the natural history of adenomatous polyps?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They typically regress spontaneously within a few years

choices.label: B
choices.text: They enlarge rapidly, growing about 5 mm per year

choices.label: D
choices.text: Essentially all of them become invasive carcinoma within 10 years

choices.label: E
choices.text: They have no malignant potential and are followed for symptoms only

explanation.summary: Adenomatous polyps grow slowly, seldom regress, and progress to cancer in only a minority of cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adenomatous polyps usually grow slowly, at an average of 0.5 mm per year, and do not commonly regress. They rarely progress to cancer, with only about 5% of cases becoming malignant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenomatous polyps do not commonly regress once they have formed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Their average growth rate is about 0.5 mm per year, an order of magnitude slower than 5 mm per year.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct: only about 5% of adenomatous polyps become malignant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Universal progression to carcinoma describes untreated familial adenomatous polyposis, not the behavior of an individual sporadic adenoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adenomatous polyps are neoplastic and do carry malignant potential, which is why they are removed and why surveillance intervals shorten.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man undergoes colonoscopy after several months of intermittent lower abdominal cramping. A 5-cm pedunculated polyp nearly filling the lumen of the sigmoid colon is identified. Most polyps of the colon produce no symptoms at all. Which of the following symptoms is most likely to result from a lesion of this size and location?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Right upper quadrant pain radiating to the scapula

explanation.summary: Most intestinal polyps are asymptomatic, but large ones can bleed or obstruct the lumen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most polyps are asymptomatic, but they may cause bleeding, pain with defecation, tenesmus when rectal, or obstruction if large. A 5-cm polyp nearly filling the sigmoid lumen is large enough to obstruct, producing cramping and obstipation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct: a large polyp can obstruct the lumen, and obstruction is the recognized complication of large polyps.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dysphagia reflects an esophageal process and cannot be produced by a sigmoid colon lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Steatorrhea reflects fat malabsorption and is not a consequence of a discrete colonic mucosal protuberance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hematemesis indicates upper gastrointestinal bleeding, whereas a sigmoid polyp that bleeds would produce blood per rectum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Right upper quadrant pain radiating to the scapula suggests biliary disease and is unrelated to a colonic polyp.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman at average risk for colorectal cancer asks about screening. She would prefer a single test that would not only detect polyps with high sensitivity and specificity but would also allow any polyps found to be removed and sent for pathologic evaluation during the same procedure. Which of the following tests best meets her request?

explanation.summary: Colonoscopy is the screening test with both diagnostic and therapeutic capability, since polyps can be removed during the examination.
explanation.whyCorrect: Colonoscopy has high sensitivity and specificity for colon cancer and offers both diagnostic and therapeutic advantages: lesions can be biopsied during the procedure and sent for pathologic evaluation, and all polyps are removed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Capsule colonoscopy uses a swallowed video capsule and cannot remove lesions; detected lesions still necessitate a colonoscopy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct: colonoscopy detects lesions with high sensitivity and specificity and allows polyps to be removed and sent for pathology in the same procedure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CT colonography is nearly as sensitive as colonoscopy but offers no therapeutic intervention, requires vigorous bowel prep, and must be repeated more frequently.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The fecal immunochemical test detects human hemoglobin in a stool sample; a positive result must be followed by timely colonoscopy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Guaiac-based fecal occult blood testing has low sensitivity for polyps and a high false-positive rate, and a positive result also requires colonoscopy.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man comes to the physician because of intermittent rectal bleeding and crampy abdominal pain for 3 months. His father died of colon cancer at 35 years of age, and a paternal aunt had colon cancer in her 30s. Colonoscopy demonstrates more than 400 adenomatous polyps carpeting the colon and rectum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Hundreds to a thousand colorectal adenomatous polyps in a young adult with an affected parent is familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP).
explanation.whyCorrect: FAP entails anywhere between 100 and 1000 colorectal adenomatous polyps and is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with near complete penetrance, matching the affected father and aunt. Most patients are diagnosed between 20 and 40 years of age and are asymptomatic until symptoms of colorectal cancer such as GI bleeding and abdominal pain appear, as in this man.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Juvenile polyposis produces hamartomatous, not adenomatous, polyps and typically becomes symptomatic by age 20 with rectal bleeding, anemia, or obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct: 100 to 1000 colorectal adenomatous polyps with autosomal dominant transmission and presentation at age 20 to 40 defines FAP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lynch syndrome was formerly called hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer and does not produce a carpet of hundreds of adenomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome causes hamartomatous polyps predominantly in the small intestine along with mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation, neither of which is described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MUTYH-associated polyposis is autosomal recessive and produces only 10 to 100 polyps, which does not fit an affected father, an affected aunt, and more than 400 polyps.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl is evaluated for recurrent crampy abdominal pain. Examination shows dark blue-brown macules on the lips, nostrils, and buccal mucosa. Endoscopy reveals multiple hamartomatous polyps, most numerous in the small intestine. Her mother has similar skin findings. A germline mutation in which of the following genes is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition caused by mutations in STK11.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome presents in childhood, with a median age of 11 years, with multiple GI hamartomatous polyps that are most numerous in the small intestine and with mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation. The dark blue to brown macules on the lips, nostrils, and buccal mucosa are characteristic, and the causative gene is STK11.

whyWrongByChoice.A: APC mutations cause familial adenomatous polyposis, which produces hundreds of adenomatous polyps rather than small bowel hamartomas with lip pigmentation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MLH1 is a DNA mismatch repair gene mutated in Lynch syndrome, which is not associated with mucocutaneous macules or hamartomatous polyps.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SMAD4 mutations cause juvenile polyposis syndrome, which produces hamartomatous polyps but is associated with congenital malformations such as pulmonary arteriovenous malformations, not mucocutaneous pigmentation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct: childhood-onset hamartomatous polyposis with mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation is Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, caused by STK11 mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MUTYH is a base excision repair gene whose biallelic mutation causes an autosomal recessive adenomatous polyposis, not hamartomatous polyps with pigmented macules.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy undergoes endoscopy for iron deficiency anemia. Multiple hamartomatous polyps are found in the jejunum and ileum, and genetic testing identifies a mutation in STK11. Which of the following physical examination findings is most likely in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blue-brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Osteomas of the skull and mandible

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sebaceous adenomas and sebaceous carcinomas of the skin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Multiple epidermoid cysts of the scalp and extremities

explanation.summary: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome pairs hamartomatous GI polyps with mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation.
explanation.whyCorrect: An STK11 mutation with multiple small intestinal hamartomatous polyps establishes Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. The associated hyperpigmentation consists of dark blue to brown macules on the lips, nostrils, buccal mucosa, palmar surfaces of the hands, genitalia, and perianal region.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct: dark blue to brown mucocutaneous macules are the hallmark external finding of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Skull osteomas occur in Gardner syndrome, a subtype of familial adenomatous polyposis, not in STK11-related disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations are among the congenital malformations seen in juvenile polyposis syndrome, which is caused by SMAD4 mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sebaceous neoplasms of the skin are among the extracolonic cancers associated with Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Epidermoid cysts are an extracolonic feature of Gardner syndrome, not Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy is evaluated for rectal bleeding and anemia. Examination shows pale conjunctivae and soft masses prolapsing from the rectum. Colonoscopy reveals numerous hamartomatous polyps throughout the colon and rectum, and genetic testing identifies a mutation in SMAD4. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medulloblastoma of the central nervous system

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation of the lips and digits

choices.label: C
choices.text: Osteomas of the skull and mandible

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sebaceous adenomas and sebaceous carcinomas of the skin

explanation.summary: Juvenile polyposis syndrome (SMAD4) is associated with congenital malformations, notably pulmonary arteriovenous malformations.
explanation.whyCorrect: Numerous hamartomatous polyps with rectal bleeding, anemia, and rectal prolapse in an adolescent with a SMAD4 mutation is juvenile polyposis syndrome. Patients also have various congenital malformations, such as pulmonary arteriovenous malformations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Brain tumors such as medulloblastoma and glioma occur in Turcot syndrome, which features adenomatous colon polyps rather than SMAD4-related hamartomas.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation belongs to Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11), a different hamartomatous polyposis syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Skull osteomas are a feature of Gardner syndrome, a subtype of familial adenomatous polyposis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sebaceous skin neoplasms are associated with Lynch syndrome and its mismatch repair gene mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct: juvenile polyposis syndrome includes congenital malformations such as pulmonary arteriovenous malformations.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman asks about inherited causes of colon cancer after her uncle was diagnosed with colorectal carcinoma at age 45. She wants to know which inherited condition she is statistically most likely to be screened for. Which of the following is the most common inherited colorectal cancer syndrome?

explanation.summary: Lynch syndrome is the most common inherited colorectal cancer syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lynch syndrome, formerly called hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, is an autosomal dominant disease caused by germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes and is the most common inherited colorectal cancer. Evaluation depends on a thorough family history, which then guides genetic testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FAP is an important autosomal dominant polyposis syndrome, but it is not the most common inherited colorectal cancer syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gardner syndrome is only a subtype of FAP and is therefore less common still.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct: Lynch syndrome is the most common inherited colorectal cancer syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant hamartomatous polyposis syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Juvenile polyposis syndrome is an uncommon hamartomatous polyposis syndrome and is not the most common inherited colorectal cancer.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is diagnosed with adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon. His mother had endometrial cancer at age 48 and his brother had colon cancer at age 42. Only two adenomatous polyps were identified at colonoscopy. A germline mutation in which of the following genes is most likely present?

explanation.summary: Lynch syndrome results from germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Right-sided colon cancer at a young age, a family history of endometrial cancer, and only a small number of polyps fit Lynch syndrome, which is autosomal dominant and caused by germline mismatch repair gene mutations. MSH2 is one of the mismatch repair genes involved, along with MLH1, MSH6, and PMS2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: APC mutations cause FAP, in which 100 to 1000 adenomatous polyps are present rather than two.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct: MSH2 is one of the DNA mismatch repair genes mutated in Lynch syndrome, which predominantly involves the right colon and increases endometrial cancer risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: STK11 mutations cause Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, characterized by hamartomatous polyps and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SMAD4 mutations cause juvenile polyposis syndrome with hamartomatous polyps presenting in adolescence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MUTYH-associated polyposis is autosomal recessive and produces 10 to 100 adenomatous polyps, which does not match this dominant-appearing family pattern.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman with genetically confirmed Lynch syndrome is scheduled for surveillance colonoscopy. Which of the following colonic segments is the most likely site of a carcinoma in this patient?

explanation.summary: Colorectal cancers in Lynch syndrome are predominantly right sided.
explanation.whyCorrect: Colorectal cancers in Lynch syndrome predominantly involve the right (ascending) colon. This right-sided predilection parallels the microsatellite instability pathway, whose tumors are also frequently located in the right colon.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The rectum is not the predominant site of Lynch syndrome carcinomas.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The sigmoid colon is a distal, left-sided segment and is not the preferential Lynch syndrome location.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The descending colon is left sided and not favored in Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct: Lynch syndrome cancers predominantly involve the right (ascending) colon.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The splenic flexure is not the site preferentially involved in Lynch syndrome.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man undergoes colonoscopy that reveals several hundred adenomatous polyps throughout the colon. Examination shows several firm bony masses over the skull and multiple epidermoid cysts on the back; imaging also demonstrates a thyroid nodule that proves to be carcinoma. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Gardner syndrome is a subtype of FAP with colonic polyposis plus osteomas, thyroid cancer, epidermoid cysts, and fibromas.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gardner syndrome, also called familial colorectal polyposis, is a subtype of FAP that presents with colonic polyps together with cancers and lesions outside the colon. Skull osteomas, thyroid cancer, and epidermoid cysts are the classic extracolonic features described here, along with fibromas.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct: adenomatous polyposis with skull osteomas, epidermoid cysts, and thyroid cancer is Gardner syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Turcot syndrome links adenomatous colon polyps with brain tumors such as medulloblastoma and glioma, none of which are described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lynch syndrome is a nonpolyposis syndrome associated with endometrial, ovarian, and sebaceous skin neoplasms rather than osteomas and epidermoid cysts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome produces hamartomatous polyps with mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation, not hundreds of adenomas with osteomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Juvenile polyposis syndrome produces hamartomatous polyps and congenital malformations such as pulmonary arteriovenous malformations.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with a history of adenomatous colonic polyposis develops progressive headache and ataxia. Imaging shows a cerebellar mass, and resection confirms medulloblastoma. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Turcot syndrome couples adenomatous colon polyps with brain tumors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Turcot syndrome is characterized by adenomatous colon polyps with an increased risk of colorectal cancer and brain cancer, specifically medulloblastoma and glioma. It may be associated with either FAP or Lynch syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gardner syndrome features osteomas of the skull, thyroid cancer, epidermoid cysts, and fibromas rather than brain tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Juvenile polyposis syndrome produces hamartomatous polyps and congenital malformations such as pulmonary arteriovenous malformations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct: adenomatous colon polyps plus medulloblastoma define Turcot syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome causes hamartomatous polyps with mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation, not adenomatous polyposis with a brain tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MUTYH-associated polyposis is an autosomal recessive adenomatous polyposis with gastric and duodenal polyps, osteomas, dental cysts, desmoids, sebaceous tumors, and thyroid cancer, not medulloblastoma.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man is found to have 45 adenomatous colonic polyps. Genetic testing identifies biallelic mutations in the MUTYH base excision repair gene. Which of the following inheritance patterns best describes this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant, with transmission in every generation

choices.label: B
choices.text: X-linked recessive, with transmission from carrier mothers to sons

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mitochondrial, with transmission from affected mothers only

choices.label: E
choices.text: Autosomal recessive, with two unaffected carrier parents

explanation.summary: MUTYH-associated polyposis is an autosomal recessive polyposis syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: MUTYH-associated polyposis is caused by mutations in the MUTYH base excision repair gene and is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. Affected individuals develop between 10 and 100 colorectal polyps, usually adenomatous, and require more frequent colorectal cancer screening.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autosomal dominant transmission characterizes FAP, Lynch syndrome, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, and juvenile polyposis, but not MUTYH-associated polyposis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: X-linked recessive inheritance is not the pattern described for any of the hereditary colon cancer syndromes discussed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: X-linked dominant inheritance does not apply to MUTYH-associated polyposis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mitochondrial inheritance does not apply to MUTYH-associated polyposis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct: MUTYH-associated polyposis is an autosomal recessive polyposis syndrome.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with familial adenomatous polyposis has more than 800 colorectal adenomatous polyps. The germline mutation responsible for her condition affects a gene on chromosome 5q21-22. The normal product of this gene functions in which of the following capacities?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Structural protein of intestinal smooth muscle

explanation.summary: FAP is caused by germline mutations in APC, a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 5q21-22.
explanation.whyCorrect: FAP is caused by germline mutations in the tumor suppressor gene APC (adenomatous polyposis coli), located on chromosome 5q21-22. Loss of this tumor suppressor drives the classic adenoma-carcinoma sequence, with both copies of APC requiring functional inactivation before adenomas develop.

whyWrongByChoice.A: KRAS is the proto-oncogene mutated later in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence; APC itself is not a proto-oncogene.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct: APC on chromosome 5q21-22 is a tumor suppressor gene, and its germline mutation causes FAP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DNA mismatch repair genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2 are mutated in Lynch syndrome, not FAP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The base excision repair gene MUTYH is mutated in autosomal recessive MUTYH-associated polyposis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Smooth muscle within the lamina propria characterizes the stroma of Peutz-Jeghers polyps but is not the function of the FAP gene product.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man with familial adenomatous polyposis undergoes serial surveillance colonoscopies. Over the past two consecutive examinations, the number of adenomatous polyps has increased markedly, and he now reports intermittent bright red blood per rectum. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Annual guaiac-based fecal occult blood testing

explanation.summary: A marked increase in polyp number and colon cancer symptoms are indications for colectomy in FAP.
explanation.whyCorrect: In FAP, prophylactic colectomy may be necessary, and the indications include development of colorectal cancer, a marked increase in the number of polyps on consecutive exams, and symptoms related to colon cancer such as GI bleeding. This patient meets two of those indications.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct: a marked rise in polyp burden on consecutive exams plus GI bleeding are explicit indications for colectomy in FAP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 10-year interval applies to average-risk screening; FAP patients require rigorous surveillance, and this patient already meets criteria for surgery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Colorectal adenocarcinoma develops in 100% of untreated FAP patients, so observation alone is inappropriate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stool-based testing has low sensitivity for polyps and would not address an escalating polyp burden with bleeding in a known FAP patient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Flexible sigmoidoscopy visualizes only the distal 60 cm of colon and does not address the indication for colectomy.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with familial adenomatous polyposis is scheduled for upper endoscopy as part of her surveillance program. Which of the following findings is most likely to be seen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inflammatory pseudopolyps of the gastric body

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gastric polyps with smooth muscle bundles arborizing through the lamina propria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hyperplastic polyps of the distal esophagus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fundic gland polyps and duodenal adenomas

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sessile serrated polyps of the gastric antrum

explanation.summary: FAP carries a high rate of upper GI tract polyps, typically fundic gland polyps and duodenal adenomas.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with FAP have a high rate of upper GI tract polyps in addition to their colorectal adenomas. These are typically fundic gland polyps and duodenal adenomas, which is why upper endoscopic surveillance is performed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inflammatory pseudopolyps form from repeated cycles of injury and healing, as in inflammatory bowel disease with mucosal erosion, not in FAP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Polyps whose stroma contains smooth muscle bundles cutting through the lamina propria are Peutz-Jeghers hamartomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperplastic polyps are colonic lesions most commonly found in the left colon and are not the characteristic upper GI finding in FAP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct: fundic gland polyps and duodenal adenomas are the typical upper GI polyps in FAP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sessile serrated polyps are colonic lesions more commonly found in the right colon and are not the expected upper GI finding in FAP.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy undergoes polypectomy of a jejunal polyp. Histologic examination shows a polyp whose surface epithelium overlies a stroma composed of bundles of smooth muscle cutting through the lamina propria. Which of the following best describes this lesion?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sessile serrated polyp with dilated crypts

explanation.summary: The Peutz-Jeghers polyp is a hamartoma with a smooth muscle stroma arborizing through the lamina propria.
explanation.whyCorrect: A Peutz-Jeghers polyp shows surface epithelium overlying stroma composed of smooth muscle bundles cutting through the lamina propria. Peutz-Jeghers polyps are hamartomatous and are most numerous in the small intestine, matching the jejunal location in an adolescent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tubular adenomas are neoplastic polyps with irregular glands and hyperchromatic, crowded nuclei with loss of goblet cells, not a smooth muscle stroma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyperplastic polyps are benign epithelial proliferations of mature goblet and absorptive cells with a serrated surface, typically small and in the left colon.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct: smooth muscle bundles cutting through the lamina propria beneath the polyp surface is the histologic signature of a Peutz-Jeghers polyp.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sessile serrated polyps show serrated architecture through the full length of the glands with crypt dilation and lateral crypt extension.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inflammatory pseudopolyps arise from repeated injury and healing with mucosal erosion, as in inflammatory bowel disease.

questions.stem: An 11-year-old girl with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is undergoing endoscopic evaluation for GI polyps. In which of the following locations are her polyps most likely to be most numerous?

explanation.summary: Peutz-Jeghers polyps follow a small intestine greater than colon greater than stomach distribution.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome presents in childhood with multiple GI hamartomatous polyps distributed as small intestine greater than colon greater than stomach. The small intestine is therefore the site with the greatest polyp burden.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The stomach is involved, but least often of the three main sites in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The rectum is not the site of greatest polyp burden in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The colon is affected, but less heavily than the small intestine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Although polyps can occur in the esophagus in general, it is not the predominant site in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct: polyps in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are most numerous in the small intestine.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman is found to carry a germline MLH1 mutation after her brother was diagnosed with Lynch syndrome. She is counseled about her risk of cancers outside the colon. Which of the following malignancies is she at greatest increased risk of developing?

explanation.summary: Lynch syndrome increases risk of endometrial, ovarian, and sebaceous skin cancers in addition to colorectal cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lynch syndrome results from germline mismatch repair gene mutations, including MLH1. Besides colorectal cancer, it increases the risk of endometrial, ovarian, and skin cancers (sebaceous neoplasms), making endometrial carcinoma the expected extracolonic malignancy in this woman.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Medulloblastoma is the brain tumor linked to Turcot syndrome, not a defining extracolonic cancer of Lynch syndrome itself.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct: endometrial carcinoma is among the extracolonic cancers whose risk is increased in Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bony lesions of the skull in these syndromes are osteomas seen in Gardner syndrome, not a Lynch-associated cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma risk is increased in juvenile polyposis syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepatocellular carcinoma is not among the malignancies associated with Lynch syndrome.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man with genetically confirmed familial adenomatous polyposis declines any surgical management and states he will not return for follow-up. Which of the following best describes his risk of colorectal adenocarcinoma if he remains untreated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nearly all patients develop colorectal adenocarcinoma by age 50

choices.label: B
choices.text: Approximately 40% of patients develop colorectal adenocarcinoma, usually after the age of 60

choices.label: C
choices.text: Approximately 5% of patients develop colorectal adenocarcinoma

choices.label: D
choices.text: His risk is no greater than that of the age-matched general population

choices.label: E
choices.text: Risk is confined to patients whose polyps show villous histology on biopsy

explanation.summary: Untreated FAP progresses to colorectal adenocarcinoma in 100% of patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Colorectal adenocarcinoma develops in 100% of untreated FAP patients, often before age 30 and nearly always by age 50. This near-certain progression is why rigorous screening and prophylactic colectomy are recommended.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct: untreated FAP progresses to colorectal adenocarcinoma in essentially all patients, often before 30 and nearly always by 50.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A malignancy risk of roughly 40% describes Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, not FAP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Roughly 5% is the proportion of sporadic adenomatous polyps that become malignant, not the cancer risk in untreated FAP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FAP carries near complete penetrance with markedly higher risk than the general population.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Villous histology raises the malignant risk of an individual adenoma but does not limit the near-universal cancer risk in FAP.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy is evaluated for 6 months of painless rectal bleeding with dark red blood mixed in the stool, fatigue, and intermittent tissue protruding from the anus. His father had surgery for intestinal polyps as a young man. Hemoglobin is low, and colonoscopy shows numerous hamartomatous polyps throughout the colon and rectum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Juvenile polyposis syndrome presents before age 20 with hamartomatous colorectal polyps, bleeding, anemia, and rectal prolapse.
explanation.whyCorrect: Juvenile polyposis syndrome is autosomal dominant, involves SMAD4 mutations, and is characterized by a few to hundreds of hamartomatous polyps. Most patients are symptomatic by age 20 with rectal bleeding, anemia, or obstruction, and may also have diarrhea or rectal prolapse, exactly as described here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FAP produces 100 to 1000 adenomatous polyps and usually presents at age 20 to 40 with symptoms of colorectal cancer, not hamartomatous polyps with prolapse in adolescence.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lynch syndrome is a nonpolyposis syndrome with right-sided colon cancer, not numerous hamartomatous colorectal polyps in a teenager.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peutz-Jeghers polyps are also hamartomatous but predominate in the small intestine and are accompanied by mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation, which is absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct: hamartomatous colorectal polyposis with bleeding, anemia, and rectal prolapse before age 20 in a dominantly affected family is juvenile polyposis syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MUTYH-associated polyposis is autosomal recessive with 10 to 100 adenomatous polyps, not dominantly transmitted hamartomatous polyposis.

questions.stem: A genetic counselor is preparing materials for families affected by hereditary colon cancer. Which of the following inheritance patterns applies to both familial adenomatous polyposis and Lynch syndrome?

explanation.summary: Both FAP and Lynch syndrome are autosomal dominant.
explanation.whyCorrect: FAP is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with near complete penetrance, and Lynch syndrome is likewise an autosomal dominant disease caused by germline mismatch repair gene mutations. Evaluation of both requires a thorough family history to guide genetic testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autosomal recessive inheritance describes MUTYH-associated polyposis, not FAP or Lynch syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neither syndrome is X-linked recessive.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct: both FAP and Lynch syndrome are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neither syndrome shows mitochondrial inheritance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neither syndrome shows X-linked dominant inheritance.

questions.stem: An 11-year-old girl is diagnosed with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome after presenting with hamartomatous small bowel polyps and pigmented macules on her lips. Her parents ask how her cancer risk should be managed. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Re-evaluation only if GI symptoms recur

choices.label: B
choices.text: First colonoscopy at age 45 with 10-year intervals thereafter

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prophylactic total colectomy at the time of diagnosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Annual guaiac-based fecal occult blood testing beginning at age 30

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lifelong cancer surveillance beginning now in childhood

explanation.summary: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome carries a high malignancy risk of about 40% and requires lifelong surveillance starting in childhood.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome carries a high malignancy risk of approximately 40%, which is why lifelong surveillance is started in childhood. This patient is already at the median age of presentation for the syndrome, so surveillance should begin now and continue for life.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Symptom-triggered evaluation alone is inadequate given an approximately 40% malignancy risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Screening beginning at age 45 with 10-year colonoscopy intervals applies to average-risk individuals, not to a child with a high-risk polyposis syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prophylactic colectomy is the operation considered in FAP for specific indications, not the recommended approach for a newly diagnosed child with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stool-based occult blood testing has low sensitivity for polyps and would not substitute for the lifelong surveillance this syndrome requires.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct: the roughly 40% malignancy risk of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome requires lifelong surveillance beginning in childhood.

questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman comes to the office for a routine health maintenance visit. She feels well and has no gastrointestinal symptoms. She has no personal history of polyps or inflammatory bowel disease, and no family member has had colorectal cancer. She takes no medications, and physical examination is unremarkable. She asks when she should begin testing for colon cancer. At which of the following ages should colorectal cancer screening begin in this patient?

explanation.summary: This item tests the age at which colorectal cancer screening begins for an average-risk adult.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient has no polyp history, no inflammatory bowel disease, and no family history of colorectal cancer, so she is at average risk. Screening for colorectal cancer typically begins at age 45 years in average-risk individuals.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Age 40 is earlier than the recommended starting point for average-risk screening; earlier initiation is reserved for patients whose risk profile differs from hers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct. Average-risk colorectal cancer screening begins at age 45 years.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Age 50 was a historic threshold, but average-risk screening now begins at 45; waiting until 50 would delay detection, particularly as diagnoses in people younger than 50 have been increasing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Age 55 would delay screening well past the recommended starting age and past the age at which most sporadic colorectal cancers begin to arise.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Age 60 would leave more than a decade of recommended screening undone in an average-risk adult.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man at average risk for colorectal cancer elects to be screened by colonoscopy. The preparation is adequate, the cecum is reached, and the entire colonic mucosa is visualized. No polyps or masses are identified, and no biopsies are taken. He has no family history of colorectal neoplasia. At which of the following intervals should this screening examination be repeated?

explanation.summary: This item tests the screening interval for colonoscopy in an average-risk patient with a normal examination.
explanation.whyCorrect: A complete colonoscopy with no polyps in an average-risk patient does not require a shortened interval. Colonoscopy performed for average-risk screening is repeated every 10 years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Annual testing is the schedule for fecal immunochemical testing, not for a normal screening colonoscopy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 3-year interval corresponds to FIT-DNA testing; it is also within the shortened range used when high-risk adenomatous polyps are found, which is not the case here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Five years is the interval for CT colonography and capsule colonoscopy, not for a normal screening colonoscopy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct. Screening colonoscopy in an average-risk patient with a normal examination is repeated every 10 years.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No colorectal cancer screening strategy uses a 15-year interval; this would leave the patient unscreened for longer than any recommended schedule.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presents to establish care and is counseled about colorectal cancer screening. He wants the test that is most likely to both detect a cancer if one is present and correctly identify disease when the test is abnormal. He has no contraindication to sedation or bowel preparation. Which of the following screening tests has the highest sensitivity and specificity for colorectal cancer?

explanation.summary: This item tests recognition of colonoscopy as the most sensitive and specific colorectal cancer screening modality.
explanation.whyCorrect: Colonoscopy has high sensitivity and high specificity for colon cancer and additionally allows biopsy and removal of any polyp encountered during the same procedure. No other screening modality matches it on both performance characteristics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct. Colonoscopy offers the highest sensitivity and specificity and also provides diagnostic and therapeutic capability.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CT colonography is nearly as sensitive as colonoscopy but does not match it, offers no therapeutic capability, and must be repeated more frequently.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flexible sigmoidoscopy examines only the distal 60 cm of the colon, so proximal lesions are missed entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The guaiac-based fecal occult blood test has low sensitivity for polyps and low specificity for disease, with a high rate of false-positive results.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The fecal immunochemical test is convenient and detects human hemoglobin in stool, but a positive result still requires colonoscopy for diagnosis, and it does not exceed colonoscopy in sensitivity or specificity.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman declines colonoscopy for colorectal cancer screening. She is instead given a kit that requires her to submit a single stool specimen each year. Her physician explains that the assay identifies blood of human origin in the sample. Which of the following best describes how this test detects disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It measures carcinoembryonic antigen shed into the stool

choices.label: B
choices.text: It requires several stool samples in order to detect intermittent bleeding

choices.label: C
choices.text: It uses specific antibodies that detect human hemoglobin in stool

choices.label: D
choices.text: It amplifies molecular markers of DNA mutations shed into the stool

choices.label: E
choices.text: It provides direct video visualization of the colonic mucosa

explanation.summary: This item tests the analytic basis of the fecal immunochemical test.
explanation.whyCorrect: A single-sample, annually performed stool test that identifies blood of human origin is the fecal immunochemical test. FIT uses specific antibodies directed against human hemoglobin, and a positive result is followed by timely colonoscopy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carcinoembryonic antigen is a serum tumor marker used to follow treated colorectal cancer, not a stool-based screening assay.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Testing several stool samples characterizes the guaiac-based fecal occult blood test; FIT usually involves only one sample.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct. FIT detects human hemoglobin in stool using specific antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Detection of molecular markers of DNA mutations describes the multitargeted FIT-DNA test, which is performed every 3 years rather than annually.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Direct video visualization of the mucosa describes capsule colonoscopy or endoscopy, not a stool-based assay.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is offered flexible sigmoidoscopy for colorectal cancer screening because he wishes to avoid an extensive bowel preparation. He asks what the main drawback of this test is compared with colonoscopy. Which of the following is the principal limitation of flexible sigmoidoscopy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It requires a more vigorous bowel preparation than colonoscopy

choices.label: B
choices.text: It must be repeated every year to be effective

choices.label: C
choices.text: It exposes the patient to ionizing radiation with each examination

choices.label: D
choices.text: It requires the patient to swallow a video capsule

choices.label: E
choices.text: It visualizes only the distal 60 cm of the colon

explanation.summary: This item tests the anatomic limitation of flexible sigmoidoscopy as a screening test.
explanation.whyCorrect: Flexible sigmoidoscopy identifies lesions only in the distal 60 cm of the colon, so more proximal neoplasms are not seen. Abnormal findings therefore require colonoscopy to visualize the entire colon.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One advantage of flexible sigmoidoscopy is that it can be performed with minimal bowel preparation; vigorous preparation is required for colonoscopy and CT colonography.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Flexible sigmoidoscopy is performed every 5 to 10 years; annual testing is the schedule for stool-based occult blood testing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Radiation exposure with repeated examinations is a concern with CT colonography, not with endoscopic sigmoidoscopy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Swallowing a double-ended video capsule describes capsule colonoscopy, a different modality.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct. Flexible sigmoidoscopy reaches only the distal 60 cm of the colon, leaving proximal lesions undetected.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman is considering CT colonography for colorectal cancer screening because she does not wish to undergo sedation. She tolerates bowel preparation well and has normal renal function. Which of the following statements about CT colonography is accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lesions identified during the study can be biopsied at the same session

choices.label: B
choices.text: Repeated examinations may increase cancer risk through cumulative radiation dose

choices.label: C
choices.text: It can be performed without any bowel preparation

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is performed at 10-year intervals, the same as colonoscopy

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is substantially less sensitive than flexible sigmoidoscopy for colonic neoplasia

explanation.summary: This item tests the advantages and disadvantages of CT colonography relative to colonoscopy.
explanation.whyCorrect: CT colonography is nearly as sensitive as colonoscopy but must be repeated more frequently than colonoscopy for adequate screening. Because each study delivers ionizing radiation, repeated examinations may raise cancer risk through cumulative dose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CT colonography is purely diagnostic; it does not offer the therapeutic interventions of colonoscopy, so identified lesions still require colonoscopy for biopsy or removal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct. CT colonography must be repeated more often than colonoscopy, and cumulative radiation from repeated studies may increase cancer risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CT colonography still requires vigorous bowel preparation, so it does not spare the patient that part of the experience.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CT colonography is performed every 5 years, not every 10 years.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CT colonography is nearly as sensitive as colonoscopy and examines the entire colon, whereas flexible sigmoidoscopy is limited to the distal 60 cm.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man undergoes screening in which he swallows a double-ended capsule containing a small video device after completing a bowel preparation. Review of the recorded images demonstrates a 12-mm sessile polyp in the ascending colon. He is asymptomatic and has no other findings. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

explanation.summary: This item tests what must follow a positive finding on a non-therapeutic screening modality.
explanation.whyCorrect: Capsule colonoscopy can detect lesions but cannot remove or sample them, so any detected lesion necessitates a colonoscopy. Colonoscopy allows the polyp to be removed and sent for pathologic evaluation, which is essential for a 12-mm polyp.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Repeating the capsule study would only re-demonstrate a lesion that is already known and would delay tissue diagnosis and removal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Stool-based testing is a screening strategy for asymptomatic patients without known lesions; it cannot characterize or remove an identified polyp.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CT colonography is another purely diagnostic study and offers no therapeutic capability, so the polyp would still remain in place.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct. A lesion detected by capsule colonoscopy requires colonoscopy, which permits biopsy and removal of the polyp.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Flexible sigmoidoscopy reaches only the distal 60 cm of the colon and would not reach a lesion in the ascending colon.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is counseled about his risk of colorectal cancer. His history includes ulcerative colitis diagnosed 25 years ago and currently controlled, a 4-mm hyperplastic polyp removed from the sigmoid colon 5 years ago, lactose intolerance, a cholecystectomy at age 40, and chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease. Which of the following elements of his history most increases his risk for colorectal carcinoma?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prior resection of a 4-mm hyperplastic polyp

explanation.summary: This item tests recognition of established risk factors for colorectal carcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inflammatory bowel disease is a recognized risk factor for colorectal cancer, along with abdominal radiation, diabetes and insulin resistance, alcohol, and processed meats. His 25-year history of ulcerative colitis is therefore the element that most raises his risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct. Inflammatory bowel disease is an established risk factor for colorectal carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyperplastic polyps are benign epithelial proliferations that lack malignant potential, and finding one does not even change the frequency of subsequent colonoscopies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactose intolerance is not among the recognized risk factors for colorectal carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prior cholecystectomy is not a recognized risk factor for colorectal carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gastroesophageal reflux disease is an upper gastrointestinal disorder and is not among the risk factors for colorectal carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is evaluated for 4 months of fatigue and exertional dyspnea. She has had no change in stool caliber, no constipation, and no abdominal distention. Laboratory studies show a microcytic anemia with a low ferritin level. Colonoscopy identifies a tumor in the ascending colon. Which of the following gross appearances is this lesion most likely to have?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An annular, constricting lesion that narrows the lumen

choices.label: B
choices.text: A small submucosal nodule composed of neuroendocrine cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: A bulky polypoid, exophytic mass projecting into the lumen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Multiple serrated polyps smaller than 5 mm confined to the mucosa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hundreds of small adenomatous polyps carpeting the entire colon

explanation.summary: This item tests the characteristic gross morphology of proximal versus distal colon cancers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumors of the proximal colon typically grow as polypoid, exophytic masses that rarely cause obstruction. That morphology explains why this patient has iron-deficiency anemia from chronic occult blood loss without any obstructive symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Annular constricting lesions that narrow the lumen are characteristic of carcinomas of the distal colon and typically produce obstructive symptoms, which she lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A small submucosal neuroendocrine nodule describes a carcinoid tumor; carcinoids present with flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm rather than iron-deficiency anemia from a colonic mass.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct. Proximal colon cancers grow as polypoid, exophytic masses that rarely obstruct and bleed occultly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Small serrated polyps are hyperplastic or sessile serrated lesions, not the invasive tumor identified in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hundreds of adenomatous polyps throughout the colon describe familial adenomatous polyposis, which presents in patients aged 20 to 40 years, not as a single mass in a 68-year-old.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man reports 3 months of progressively worsening constipation, narrow-caliber stools, and crampy lower abdominal pain relieved by passing flatus. He has had intermittent bright red blood per rectum. Colonoscopy cannot be advanced past a lesion in the sigmoid colon, and biopsy shows invasive adenocarcinoma. Which of the following gross features of this tumor best accounts for his symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A polypoid, exophytic mass growing into a wide lumen

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 4-mm hyperplastic polyp with serrated surface architecture

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inflammatory pseudopolyps arising from repeated mucosal erosion

choices.label: E
choices.text: An annular lesion producing constriction and luminal narrowing

explanation.summary: This item tests the link between distal colon cancer morphology and obstructive symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carcinomas in the distal colon tend to be annular lesions that produce constrictions and luminal narrowing. Progressive constipation, narrow-caliber stools, and crampy pain in a patient whose sigmoid lesion cannot be traversed reflect exactly that growth pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Polypoid, exophytic growth is typical of proximal colon tumors and rarely causes obstruction; it more often presents with occult blood loss and anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A hyperplastic polyp is a small benign epithelial proliferation without malignant potential and would not obstruct the lumen or explain an invasive adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An appendiceal neuroendocrine tumor is a carcinoid, not a colonic adenocarcinoma, and would not produce a non-traversable sigmoid stricture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inflammatory pseudopolyps arise in inflammatory bowel disease from repeated cycles of injury and healing and are non-neoplastic, so they would not yield invasive adenocarcinoma on biopsy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct. Distal colon carcinomas typically form annular, constricting lesions that narrow the lumen and cause obstructive symptoms.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman undergoes resection of a sigmoid adenocarcinoma. The pathology report describes a moderately differentiated gland-forming tumor, its depth of penetration through the bowel wall, the status of 18 regional lymph nodes, tumor size, and the gross configuration of the lesion. Which of the following pairs of findings is most important in determining her prognosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tumor size and gross configuration of the lesion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depth of invasion and presence of lymph node metastases

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum carcinoembryonic antigen level and patient age

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polyp shape and segment of colon involved

choices.label: E
choices.text: Presence of goblet cells and degree of mucin production

explanation.summary: This item tests the two most important prognostic factors in colorectal adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The two most important prognostic factors for colorectal adenocarcinoma are the depth of invasion and the presence of lymph node metastases. Both are supplied by the resection specimen and drive staging and subsequent management.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tumor size and gross configuration correlate with location and presenting symptoms but are not the dominant prognostic determinants.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct. Depth of invasion and lymph node metastasis are the two most important prognostic factors in colorectal adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carcinoembryonic antigen is used to follow response after treatment rather than as a primary prognostic determinant, and age alone does not define prognosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polyp shape is relevant to estimating malignant potential of a precursor lesion, not to prognosis after an invasive cancer is resected.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mucinous differentiation is characteristic of microsatellite-unstable, right-sided tumors, but it is not one of the two dominant prognostic factors.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man is reluctant to undergo colonoscopy and asks whether a simple blood test could be used instead to check him for colon cancer. He is asymptomatic, and his physical examination is normal. Which of the following statements about carcinoembryonic antigen best answers his question?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the most sensitive available test for detecting early colorectal cancer

choices.label: B
choices.text: It can replace colonoscopy in patients who are unwilling to undergo bowel preparation before screening

choices.label: C
choices.text: An elevated level is diagnostic of colorectal carcinoma

choices.label: D
choices.text: It lacks sensitivity for early disease and is used to follow treatment response

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is used to determine the age at which screening should begin

explanation.summary: This item tests the appropriate clinical role of carcinoembryonic antigen in colorectal cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carcinoembryonic antigen is the main tumor marker associated with colon cancer, but it should not be used as a screening test because of low sensitivity and specificity for early-stage disease. It is instead used around the time of treatment to monitor response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Colonoscopy, not carcinoembryonic antigen, is the most sensitive and specific test for colorectal cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Because it performs poorly in early-stage disease, carcinoembryonic antigen cannot substitute for a structural examination of the colon.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An elevated level is not diagnostic; specificity is low, and diagnosis requires tissue obtained at colonoscopy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct. Carcinoembryonic antigen lacks the sensitivity and specificity needed for screening and is used to follow treatment response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The age at which screening begins is determined by risk status, not by a tumor marker level.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is found on colonoscopy to have a mass in the descending colon, and biopsy confirms invasive colorectal adenocarcinoma. He is otherwise well, and his physical examination shows no palpable masses or lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in his pretreatment evaluation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flexible sigmoidoscopy to reassess the distal colon and rectum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat colonoscopy in 1 year for surveillance

choices.label: E
choices.text: Initiation of annual fecal immunochemical testing

explanation.summary: This item tests the components of pretreatment clinical staging in colorectal adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once invasive colorectal adenocarcinoma is diagnosed, optimal management includes pretreatment clinical staging with physical examination, CT of the abdomen and pelvis, and chest imaging. These studies define the extent of disease before therapy is chosen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct. Pretreatment staging includes physical examination, CT of the abdomen and pelvis, and chest imaging.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The lesion has already been visualized and biopsied at colonoscopy, and sigmoidoscopy adds nothing to staging beyond the distal 60 cm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Capsule colonoscopy is a screening modality with no therapeutic or staging capability and would not assess extracolonic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Delaying evaluation for a year is inappropriate once invasive carcinoma has been confirmed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stool-based screening is for asymptomatic individuals without known disease and has no role after a cancer diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man is diagnosed with colorectal adenocarcinoma. Staging studies show tumor invading the bowel wall with involvement of two regional lymph nodes and no distant metastases. He wishes to know which treatment offers him the chance of cure. Which of the following modalities is curative in this setting?

explanation.summary: This item tests the only curative modality for colorectal adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 80% of colon cancers are localized to the colon wall and/or regional lymph nodes, and in that setting surgical resection is the only curative modality. Systemic therapy is added afterward as clinically indicated rather than used in place of surgery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adjuvant systemic therapy is given after resection as clinically indicated; by itself it is not curative.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immune checkpoint inhibitors benefit patients whose tumors show microsatellite instability, but they supplement rather than replace resection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct. Surgical resection is the only curative modality for disease confined to the bowel wall and regional nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Somatostatin analogs are used for symptomatic or metastatic carcinoid tumors, not for colorectal adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Abdominal radiation is itself listed among the risk factors for colorectal cancer and is not the curative treatment for this disease.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman is found to have an adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon. Histology shows prominent mucinous differentiation with a dense peritumoral lymphoid infiltrate, and molecular testing demonstrates microsatellite instability with loss of mismatch repair protein expression. Which of the following therapies is she most likely to benefit from?

explanation.summary: This item tests the therapeutic implication of microsatellite instability in colorectal cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mucinous differentiation, peritumoral lymphoid infiltrates, and a right-sided location are the hallmarks of tumors arising through the microsatellite instability pathway. Patients with microsatellite instability tumors may benefit from neoadjuvant immunotherapy because these tumors respond to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Somatostatin analogs are used for symptomatic or metastatic carcinoid tumors, not for colorectal adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Niacin supplementation addresses the vitamin B3 deficiency associated with carcinoid syndrome and has no antitumor role here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prophylactic colectomy is a strategy for polyposis syndromes such as familial adenomatous polyposis, not for an established single carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CT colonography is a screening modality, not a treatment, and offers no therapeutic capability.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct. Microsatellite instability tumors respond to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man is evaluated for 3 months of fatigue. He reports no melena, no hematochezia, and no abdominal pain. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL with a low mean corpuscular volume and a low serum ferritin level. He has never undergone colorectal cancer screening. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Empiric oral iron with repeat blood count in 3 months

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reassurance with screening deferred to age 65

explanation.summary: This item tests the significance of iron-deficiency anemia in an adult man.
explanation.whyCorrect: Iron-deficiency anemia in an adult male or a post-menopausal female is colon cancer until proven otherwise. Because colorectal cancer often bleeds occultly and produces no other symptoms until advanced, colonoscopy is required to visualize the entire colon and biopsy any lesion found.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Treating the anemia empirically would mask the finding that prompted concern and delay diagnosis of a potentially curable cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct. Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia in an adult man mandates colonoscopy to exclude colorectal cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Guaiac testing has low sensitivity for polyps and low specificity for disease, and a negative result would not exclude cancer in a patient who already has objective evidence of blood loss.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carcinoembryonic antigen has low sensitivity and specificity for early-stage disease and should not be used to detect cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Deferring evaluation ignores an abnormal finding; screening schedules apply to asymptomatic patients without evidence of blood loss.

questions.stem: A physician is preparing educational material describing how colorectal carcinoma comes to medical attention. She notes that most patients with early-stage disease have no symptoms, and that once symptoms appear the disease is usually relatively advanced. Which of the following is the most common presenting symptom of colorectal carcinoma?

explanation.summary: This item tests the most frequent presenting symptom of colorectal carcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Changes in bowel habits are the most common symptom associated with colorectal cancer, occurring about 74% of the time. Rectal bleeding together with altered bowel movements is the most common combination of symptoms, but altered bowel habits is the single most frequent complaint.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abdominal pain as the only presenting symptom of colorectal cancer is rare.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An abdominal mass can be a presenting finding but is far less common than altered bowel habits.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A rectal mass is a recognized presentation but occurs much less often than a change in bowel habits.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct. Change in bowel habits is reported in roughly 74% of patients, making it the most common presenting symptom.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Flushing and bronchospasm are features of carcinoid syndrome from a metastatic neuroendocrine tumor, not of colorectal adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman reports 2 years of episodic facial flushing, often provoked by alcohol or a heavy meal, accompanied by watery diarrhea and intermittent wheezing. CT imaging demonstrates a mass in the distal ileum along with multiple hepatic lesions. Biopsy of a liver lesion shows a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor. Excess secretion of which of the following substances is the most likely cause of her symptoms?

explanation.summary: This item tests the vasoactive mediator responsible for carcinoid syndrome in midgut tumors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Midgut carcinoid tumors of the jejunum, ileum, appendix, and ascending colon secrete kallikrein, prostaglandins, and serotonin and classically produce carcinoid syndrome. Systemic symptoms such as flushing occur when a small bowel tumor metastasizes to the liver, as it has here, and episodes are typically triggered by stress, food, or alcohol.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct. Serotonin is the vasoactive substance secreted by midgut carcinoid tumors that produces flushing, diarrhea, and bronchospasm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Histamine is secreted by foregut tumors of the stomach and duodenum, which only rarely produce carcinoid syndrome, and her tumor is ileal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Insulin excess produces hypoglycemic symptoms, not episodic flushing, secretory diarrhea, and bronchospasm.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gastrin is not among the vasoactive substances responsible for carcinoid syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Somatostatin analogs are used to treat this syndrome; somatostatin excess does not cause flushing and bronchospasm.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with a metastatic midgut neuroendocrine tumor and long-standing episodic flushing and diarrhea now has a scaly, hyperpigmented rash over sun-exposed skin of his neck and forearms, worsening diarrhea, and new memory impairment and confusion noted by his wife. Deficiency of which of the following vitamins best explains these new findings?

explanation.summary: This item tests the nutritional deficiency associated with carcinoid syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carcinoid syndrome is associated with vitamin B3 (niacin) deficiency. Niacin deficiency causes pellagra, whose clinical hallmark is the triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia, exactly the combination described here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vitamin B12 deficiency is not the deficiency associated with carcinoid syndrome and does not produce the dermatitis-diarrhea-dementia triad.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin A deficiency is not linked to carcinoid syndrome in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct. Carcinoid syndrome causes niacin deficiency, producing pellagra with dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin D deficiency is not the deficiency associated with carcinoid syndrome and does not explain this triad.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Folate deficiency is not the deficiency associated with carcinoid syndrome and does not produce photosensitive dermatitis with dementia.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman has a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor of the ileum with extensive bilobar hepatic metastases that are not amenable to resection. She has disabling flushing and up to eight watery stools daily. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for her symptoms?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Annual guaiac-based fecal occult blood testing

explanation.summary: This item tests the management of symptomatic or metastatic carcinoid tumors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carcinoid tumors are managed with surgical resection when localized and with somatostatin analogs for symptomatic or metastatic disease. Because her hepatic metastases are unresectable and she has disabling flushing and diarrhea, somatostatin analog therapy is appropriate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Colectomy would not address an ileal primary with unresectable hepatic metastases and is a strategy used for polyposis syndromes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immune checkpoint inhibitors benefit colorectal tumors with microsatellite instability, not well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carcinoembryonic antigen is the tumor marker used to follow colorectal adenocarcinoma after treatment and would not relieve any of her symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stool occult blood testing is a colorectal cancer screening test and has no role in treating symptomatic metastatic carcinoid disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct. Somatostatin analogs are used for symptomatic or metastatic carcinoid tumors.

questions.stem: A term male newborn is delivered to a 27-year-old woman who received no prenatal care. On examination there is a 4-cm midline defect at the base of the umbilical cord through which loops of bowel and a portion of the liver protrude. The protruding organs are enclosed within a thin, nearly transparent membrane that is intact. Echocardiography performed on the first day of life shows a ventricular septal defect. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Recognition of omphalocele: a central defect through the umbilical ring with viscera enclosed in a thin, nearly transparent sac and frequent associated anomalies.
explanation.whyCorrect: In omphalocele the infant's intestines, liver, or other organs protrude through the umbilical ring and are covered by a thin, nearly transparent sac that is usually intact at birth. Infants with omphalocele often have other birth defects such as cardiac anomalies, which fits the ventricular septal defect found here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastroschisis produces free loops of bowel that are not covered by a sac or skin and the defect lies beside the umbilicus, not centrally through the umbilical ring.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct. A central defect at the base of the cord with viscera in a thin translucent sac, plus an associated cardiac defect, defines omphalocele.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An umbilical hernia is covered by normal skin rather than a translucent membrane and usually appears after birth rather than being present at delivery with liver outside the abdomen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Patent urachus presents with urine leaking from the umbilicus, not with herniated abdominal viscera.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An epigastric hernia occurs in the midline between the xiphoid process and the umbilicus and does not present as a neonatal sac-covered mass at the cord insertion.

questions.stem: A term newborn is noted immediately after delivery to have loops of intestine protruding through a 3-cm full-thickness defect in the anterior abdominal wall located immediately to the right of a normally inserted umbilical cord. The exposed bowel is not covered by a membrane or by skin. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Recognition of gastroschisis: uncovered viscera herniating through an anterior abdominal wall defect adjacent to the umbilicus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gastroschisis is herniation of abdominal organs through a defect in the anterior abdominal wall adjacent to the umbilicus, and the organs are not covered by a sac or skin. Free-floating bowel loops beside a normally inserted cord, typically on the right, are characteristic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Omphalocele herniates centrally through the umbilical ring and the contents are enclosed in a thin, nearly transparent membranous sac.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An umbilical hernia is a skin-covered protrusion at the umbilical ring that generally becomes apparent after birth, not exposed bowel at delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Patent urachus causes urine drainage from the umbilicus and does not produce herniated viscera.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct. Uncovered bowel protruding through a wall defect beside the umbilical cord is the defining presentation of gastroschisis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spigelian hernias protrude through the Spigelian fascia at the lateral edge of the rectus muscle and are not a neonatal defect with exposed bowel at the cord.

questions.stem: A newborn is found to have uncovered loops of intestine protruding through an opening in the anterior abdominal wall just beside the umbilical cord. There is no membrane over the exposed bowel. Which of the following developmental events best explains this defect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Persistence of the processus vaginalis after testicular descent

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of the herniated midgut to return to the abdominal cavity by the 10th to 11th week of gestation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of the lateral folds to fuse in the midline during week 4

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of the umbilical ring to close during the first years after birth

choices.label: E
choices.text: Failure of the urachus to obliterate after fetal bladder drainage

explanation.summary: Embryologic basis of gastroschisis: failed midline fusion of the lateral abdominal wall components during week 4.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gastroschisis arises in week 4 from failure of fusion of the right and left anterior abdominal wall components in the midline during lateral folding. The result is a full-thickness wall defect beside the umbilicus through which viscera protrude with no covering sac.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A persistent processus vaginalis predisposes to indirect inguinal hernias, not to a paraumbilical wall defect with exposed bowel.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Failure of the intestines to return to the abdomen by the 10th or 11th week produces an omphalocele, in which the contents are covered by a thin translucent sac.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct. Gastroschisis results from week 4 failure of midline fusion of the right and left abdominal wall components during lateral folding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Failure or weakening of umbilical ring closure combined with increased intra-abdominal pressure produces an umbilical hernia, which is skin covered and appears after birth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A patent urachus causes urine drainage from the umbilicus rather than herniation of uncovered bowel.

questions.stem: A term newborn has abdominal viscera protruding centrally through the umbilical ring. The herniated organs are enclosed within a thin, nearly transparent sac that is intact. Which of the following developmental events best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Failure of the right and left lateral abdominal wall folds to fuse in the midline during week 4 of gestation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Persistence of the processus vaginalis after testicular descent

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of the umbilical ring to close during the first years of life

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of the urachus to obliterate after fetal bladder drainage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Failure of the herniated midgut to return to the abdominal cavity by week 10 to 11

explanation.summary: Embryologic basis of omphalocele: the intestines fail to return to the abdomen at the expected point in gestation.
explanation.whyCorrect: By the 10th or 11th week of pregnancy the intestines normally return into the abdomen; if they do not, an omphalocele results. The retained viscera remain at the umbilical ring enclosed in a thin, nearly transparent sac, exactly as described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Failure of lateral fold fusion in week 4 causes gastroschisis, in which viscera protrude beside the umbilicus with no covering sac.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A persistent processus vaginalis underlies indirect inguinal hernias, not a sac-covered defect at the umbilical ring.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failure of umbilical ring closure after birth produces an umbilical hernia covered by normal skin, not a translucent membrane present at delivery.
